1.solution: \(99\) g of \(\mathrm{CO_2}\) is \(\dfrac{99}{44} = 2.25\) mol. At STP one mole occupies \(22.4\) L, so the volume is \(2.25 \times 22.4 = 50.4\) L.

2.solution: Argon is \(1s^2\,2s^2\,2p^6\,3s^2\,3p^6\). The s orbitals hold \(2 + 2 + 2 = 6\) electrons and the p orbitals \(6 + 6 = 12\).

3.subtopic: Group 16 Chalcogens, Oxygen, Sulphur and Ozone
3.solution: Down group 16 the E-H bond grows longer and weaker, so the hydride releases \(\mathrm{H^+}\) more easily. Acidity rises from \(\mathrm{H_2O}\) to \(\mathrm{H_2Te}\), which is the most acidic.

4.subtopic: Ionic and Covalent Bonding, Lewis Structures and Octet Rule
4.solution: In a salt such as \(\mathrm{[R_4N]^+X^-}\), three N-R bonds are ordinary covalent bonds and the fourth is formed when N donates its lone pair (a co-ordinate bond). The cation and the anion \(\mathrm{X^-}\) are held by an ionic bond. All three types are present.

5.subtopic: Gas Laws and Ideal Gas Equation

7.subtopic: Thermochemistry, Hess's Law and Bond Enthalpy
7.solution:
For \(\dfrac{1}{2}\mathrm{H_2} + \dfrac{1}{2}\mathrm{Cl_2} \rightarrow \mathrm{HCl}\): bonds broken \(= \dfrac{1}{2}(434) + \dfrac{1}{2}(242) = 338\) kJ, bond formed \(= 431\) kJ.

\(\Delta_f H = 338 - 431 = -93\ \mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}}\).

8.subtopic: pH, pOH and Ionic Product of Water
8.solution: \(\dfrac{2.8}{56} = 0.05\) mol in \(0.5\) L gives \([\mathrm{OH^-}] = 0.1\) M (KOH is a strong base). \(\mathrm{pOH} = 1\), so \(\mathrm{pH} = 14 - 1 = 13\).

10.solution: Blood is buffered (mainly by the carbonic acid-bicarbonate system) at a pH of about \(7.4\), slightly basic.

12.subtopic: Group 2 Alkaline Earth Metals, Properties and Reactivity
12.solution: The small \(\mathrm{Mg^{2+}}\) ion polarises the large carbonate ion most strongly, weakening it. Thermal stability of the carbonates rises down the group, so \(\mathrm{MgCO_3}\) decomposes most easily.

13.subtopic: IUPAC Nomenclature, Functional Groups and Homologous Series
13.solution: Successive members differ by one \(\mathrm{CH_2}\) unit (\(14\) g/mol). The second and fourth members differ by two such units: \(28\) g/mol.

14.subtopic: Reactions of Alkenes, Addition, Oxidation and Ozonolysis
14.solution: Acidified permanganate breaks the C=C bond and oxidises each end to COOH. In a ring both ends belong to the same chain, so the ring opens into a six-carbon chain with COOH at each end: hexane-1,6-dioic acid (adipic acid).

15.subtopic: Side-Chain Reactions, Oxidation and Other Transformations
15.solution: In the Wurtz-Fittig reaction an aryl halide and an alkyl halide are coupled with sodium in dry ether: \(\mathrm{C_6H_5Br + CH_3Br + 2Na \rightarrow C_6H_5CH_3 + 2NaBr}\). The other three make alkyl or aryl halides.

16.subtopic: First Law of Thermodynamics, Internal Energy and Work
16.solution:
\(\mathrm{C_2H_4 + HCl \rightarrow C_2H_5Cl}\) uses equal volumes, so HCl (\(150\) mL) is limiting: \(150\) mL of ethylene and \(150\) mL of HCl give \(150\) mL of product. The gas volume falls by \(150\) mL.

\(W = -P\Delta V = -(1 \times 10^5\ \mathrm{Pa})(-150 \times 10^{-6}\ \mathrm{m^3}) = +15\) J (work is done on the system).

17.solution: Ethene, ethyne and cyclohexene add bromine across their multiple bonds and decolourise bromine water. Benzene's delocalised \(\pi\) system is stable and does not add bromine under these conditions.

18.subtopic: Types of Solids, Crystal Systems and Properties
18.solution:
A: \(7\) corners \(\times \dfrac{1}{8} = \dfrac{7}{8}\). B: \(6\) faces \(\times \dfrac{1}{2} = 3\).

\(\mathrm{A_{7/8}B_3}\), multiplied by 8: \(\mathrm{A_7B_{24}}\).

20.solution: fcc is a cubic close-packed structure: each sphere touches 6 in its own layer, 3 above and 3 below, a coordination number of \(12\).

21.subtopic: Types of Solutions, Solubility and Henry's Law
21.solution: Sea water is salt (a solid) dissolved in water (a liquid). Hydrogen in palladium is a gas in a solid, and gels and amalgams are liquids in solids.

23.subtopic: Types of Solutions, Solubility and Henry's Law
23.solution: Henry's law in this form is \(S = K_H P = 0.15 \times 0.18 = 0.027\) M.

24.subtopic: Galvanic Cells, EMF, Nernst Equation and Thermodynamics

25.subtopic: Molar Conductivity, Kohlrausch's Law and Degree of Dissociation
25.solution: Dilution leaves fewer ions per unit volume, so the conductivity \(\kappa\) falls. Molar conductivity refers to one mole of electrolyte, and on dilution the ions move more freely (and weak electrolytes dissociate more), so \(\Lambda\) rises.

26.solution:
A: \(\mathrm{2H_2O \rightarrow O_2 + 4H^+ + 4e^-}\), so \(2\) F per mole of water (II).

B: Mn goes from \(+7\) to \(+2\), \(5\) F (IV).

C: \(\mathrm{Ca^{2+} + 2e^- \rightarrow Ca}\); for \(1.5\) mol, \(3\) F (I).

D: Fe goes from \(+2\) to \(+3\), \(1\) F (III).

27.subtopic: First-Order Kinetics, Rate Constant and Half-Life

28.subtopic: First-Order Kinetics, Rate Constant and Half-Life

29.subtopic: Rate Law, Order, Molecularity and Rate Expression
29.solution: Order is read from the experimental rate law, not from the balanced equation. Rate \(= k[\mathrm{H_2O_2}]^1\), so the reaction is first order.

30.solution: A material small in all three dimensions is zero-dimensional: nanoparticles, quantum dots and nanoshells. Nanotubes and nanowires are long in one dimension, and thin films extend in two.

31.solution: Gases that liquefy easily, those with a high critical temperature, have stronger van der Waals forces and are adsorbed more. \(\mathrm{SO_2}\) has by far the highest critical temperature of the four, so it is adsorbed most.

32.subtopic: Group 18 Noble Gases and Xenon Compounds
32.solution:
\(\mathrm{XeF_4}\): 4 bond pairs and 2 lone pairs, square planar (ii).

\(\mathrm{XeF_6}\): 6 bond pairs and 1 lone pair, distorted octahedral (iii).

\(\mathrm{XeOF_4}\): 5 bonded atoms and 1 lone pair, square pyramidal (iv).

\(\mathrm{XeO_3}\): 3 bonded atoms and 1 lone pair, pyramidal (i).

33.subtopic: Inner Transition Elements, Lanthanoids and Actinoids
33.solution: Promethium (Pm, \(Z = 61\)) has no stable isotope; it is the only radioactive lanthanoid.

34.subtopic: Position, Electronic Configuration and General Features of d-Block
34.solution: Cobalt (\(Z = 27\)) is in the first transition series (3d) and molybdenum (\(Z = 42\)) in the second (4d).

35.solution: An ambidentate ligand can bind through either of two different atoms. Thiocyanate binds through S (\(\mathrm{SCN^-}\)) or through N (\(\mathrm{NCS^-}\)). Ethylenediamine and EDTA are chelating ligands, and \(\mathrm{Cl^-}\) has only one donor atom.

36.solution: The ambidentate ligands here are \(\mathrm{NO_2^-}\) (N or O) and \(\mathrm{NCS^-}\) (N or S). Set (B), oxalate, ethylenediamine and water, has neither.

37.subtopic: Colour, Magnetic Properties and Spin-Only Formula
37.solution: A compound shows the complementary colour of the light it absorbs. The complement of red is blue-green, so the compound appears blue.

38.subtopic: Polyhalogen Compounds — Freon, DDT, War Gases
38.solution: Air and light slowly oxidise chloroform to the poisonous gas phosgene: \(\mathrm{2CHCl_3 + O_2 \rightarrow 2COCl_2 + 2HCl}\).

39.solution: By Saytzeff's rule the more substituted alkene is the major product. Removing H from \(\mathrm{C_3}\) gives but-2-ene, \(\mathrm{CH_3CH{=}CHCH_3}\) (but-1-ene is the minor product).

40.solution: \(\mathrm{C_6H_5OH}\) is acidic enough to dissolve in NaOH, gives a violet colour with neutral ferric chloride, and with bromine water gives 2,4,6-tribromophenol. The compound is phenol.

41.subtopic: Chemical Reactions of Alcohols and Acidity
41.solution: With concentrated \(\mathrm{H_2SO_4}\) at about \(413\) K, the alcohol is protonated, and a second alcohol molecule attacks it, displacing water in one step: an \(\mathrm{S_N2}\) reaction. (This route works for primary alcohols.)

42.subtopic: IUPAC and Common Nomenclature of Alcohols, Phenols and Ethers
42.solution: The \(\mathrm{C_4H_9OH}\) alcohols are butan-1-ol and 2-methylpropan-1-ol (primary), butan-2-ol (secondary) and 2-methylpropan-2-ol (tertiary). Two are primary.

43.subtopic: Diazonium Salts and Aromatic Amine Reactions
43.solution: In the Gattermann reaction a benzenediazonium salt is converted to an aryl halide with copper powder and the halogen acid (HBr or HCl). CO, HCl and anhydrous \(\mathrm{AlCl_3}\) belong to the Gattermann-Koch formylation, a different reaction.

44.solution:
Cross products come from the enolate of one aldehyde adding to the other.

Enolate of ethanal adding to propanal: \(\mathrm{CH_3CH_2CH(OH)CH_2CHO}\), which dehydrates to \(\mathrm{CH_3CH_2CH{=}CHCHO}\), pent-2-enal.

Enolate of propanal adding to ethanal: \(\mathrm{CH_3CH(OH)CH(CH_3)CHO}\), which dehydrates to \(\mathrm{CH_3CH{=}C(CH_3)CHO}\), 2-methylbut-2-enal.

(But-2-enal and 2-methylpent-2-enal are the self-condensation products.)

45.solution: Friedel-Crafts acylation uses an acid chloride, \(\mathrm{RCOCl}\), with anhydrous \(\mathrm{AlCl_3}\): the acid chloride gives the acylium ion \(\mathrm{RC{\equiv}O^+}\) that attacks the ring. Esters, acids and ketones do not form the electrophile this way.
45.note: the four printed option structures are written as LaTeX formulas; no figure needed

46.subtopic: Glycosidic Linkages in Di- and Polysaccharides
46.solution: Maltose is two \(\alpha\)-D-glucose units joined by an \(\alpha\)-1,4 glycosidic link, a disaccharide.

47.solution: Buna-S (styrene-butadiene rubber) is a synthetic rubber: an elastomer, stretched under force and returning to shape when released.

48.solution: Teflon is polytetrafluoroethene, made from tetrafluoroethene, \(\mathrm{CF_2{=}CF_2}\).

49.solution: Enzymes are highly specific, each catalysing a particular reaction or substrate. Like any catalyst they lower the activation energy, leave the equilibrium constant unchanged and are not used up.

50.subtopic: Colloids, Classification, Coagulation and Hardy-Schulze Rule
50.solution: \(\mathrm{Ca^{2+}}\) and \(\mathrm{Mg^{2+}}\) in hard water precipitate soap as insoluble calcium and magnesium salts of the fatty acids, which appear as scum.

51.subtopic: Algebra of Complex Numbers — Conjugates, Powers of i and Cube Roots of Unity
51.solution:
The roots are \(\omega\) and \(\omega^2\), with \(\omega^3 = 1\). Since \(2026 = 3 \times 675 + 1\), \(\omega^{2026} = \omega\) and \((\omega^2)^{2026} = \omega^{4052} = \omega^2\) (as \(4052 = 3 \times 1350 + 2\)).

Sum \(= \omega + \omega^2 = -1\).

52.solution: \(n\) different things round a circle can be arranged in \((n - 1)!\) ways, and a necklace can be turned over, so clockwise and anticlockwise orders are the same: \(\dfrac{7!}{2} = 2520\).

53.subtopic: Solution of Triangle — Sine, Cosine and Projection Rules
53.solution:
With \(A = 90^\circ\), a is the hypotenuse: \(\sin B = \cos C = \dfrac{b}{a}\) and \(\cos B = \sin C = \dfrac{c}{a}\).

\(\sin(B - C) = \sin B\cos C - \cos B\sin C = \dfrac{b^2 - c^2}{a^2} = \dfrac{b^2 - c^2}{b^2 + c^2}\).

55.solution:
\(\cos 4\theta = \cos 3\theta\) gives \(4\theta = 2n\pi \pm 3\theta\), that is \(\theta = 2n\pi\) or \(\theta = \dfrac{2n\pi}{7}\).

Every \(2n\pi\) is also of the form \(\dfrac{2m\pi}{7}\) (take \(m = 7n\)), so the general solution is \(\theta = \dfrac{2n\pi}{7}\).

56.solution: \(A = (2, 0)\) and \(B = (0, 4)\). If AC is perpendicular to BC, the angle at C is a right angle, so C lies on the circle with AB as diameter. Its distance from the midpoint of AB is the radius, \(\dfrac{AB}{2} = \dfrac{\sqrt{4 + 16}}{2} = \sqrt{5}\).

57.subtopic: General Second-Degree Equation — Condition for a Pair, Parallel Lines and Distances
57.solution: \((x - 2y)(x - 2y + k) = 0\) gives the parallel lines \(x - 2y = 0\) and \(x - 2y + k = 0\). Their distance is \(\dfrac{k}{\sqrt{5}} = 3\), so \(k = 3\sqrt{5}\).

58.subtopic: Slopes of a Homogeneous Pair — Sum, Product and Ratio Conditions
58.solution:
Compare with \(Ax^2 + 2Hxy + By^2 = 0\): \(A = \dfrac{1}{a}\), \(H = \dfrac{1}{h}\), \(B = \dfrac{1}{b}\). The slopes satisfy \(m_1 + m_2 = -\dfrac{2H}{B}\) and \(m_1m_2 = \dfrac{A}{B}\).

With \(m_2 = 2m_1\): \(3m_1 = -\dfrac{2H}{B}\) and \(2m_1^2 = \dfrac{A}{B}\). Eliminating \(m_1\): \(\dfrac{8H^2}{9B^2} = \dfrac{A}{B}\), so \(8H^2 = 9AB\).

\(\dfrac{8}{h^2} = \dfrac{9}{ab}\), hence \(h^2 : ab = 8 : 9\).

59.subtopic: Equation of a Circle — Centre-Radius, General, Diameter and Parametric Forms
59.solution:
A circle has no xy term and equal \(x^2\), \(y^2\) coefficients: \(p = 3\) and \(q = 3\).

The equation becomes \(3x^2 + 3y^2 - 6x = 72\), that is \(x^2 + y^2 - 2x = 24\), or \((x - 1)^2 + y^2 = 25\). The radius is 5 and the area \(25\pi\).

61.subtopic: Algebraic Limits — Factorisation, Rationalisation and the xⁿ − aⁿ Form

62.solution:
(A) holds for \(x = 6\), (B) for \(x = 1\) and (D) for \(x = 1\).

(C) needs \(x \ge 4\) for every x, but \(1 + 6 = 7 < 10\). So (C) is not true.

63.solution:
\(p \to q\) is false only when p is T and q is F; then \(p \vee q\) is T. So statement r is false.

\(p \leftrightarrow q\) is false when exactly one of p, q is T; then \(p \vee q\) is T. So statement s is false.

\(r \to s\): F \(\to\) F is T. \(s \to r\): F \(\to\) F is T.

64.subtopic: Solution of Triangle — Sine, Cosine and Projection Rules
64.solution:
Angles in AP sum to \(\pi\), so the middle one is \(B = \dfrac{\pi}{3}\).

\(\dfrac{c}{b} = \sqrt{\dfrac{2}{3}}\), so by the sine rule \(\sin C = \sqrt{\dfrac{2}{3}} \times \dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2} = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\). Since \(C < \pi - B\), \(C = \dfrac{\pi}{4}\).

\(A = \pi - \dfrac{\pi}{3} - \dfrac{\pi}{4} = \dfrac{5\pi}{12}\).

65.subtopic: Inverse of a Matrix — Adjoint Formula, Products and Verification
65.solution:
Multiplying out, \(A^2 = I\), so \(A^{-1} = A\).

Then (A) would need \(A^2 = A\), which is false; \(|A| = 1\), so \(\mathrm{adj}A = |A|A^{-1} = A\) and (B) is false; (D) would need \(A^2 = -I\), false.

66.subtopic: Systems of Linear Equations and Symmetric, Skew-Symmetric Matrices
66.solution:
The system is \(2a + b - c = 4\), \(-a + 2b + c = 0\), \(a - b + 2c = -2\).

From the second, \(c = a - 2b\). The first gives \(a + 3b = 4\) and the third \(3a - 5b = -2\). So \(b = 1\), \(a = 1\), \(c = -1\).

Distance of \((1, 1, -1)\) from the plane \(= \dfrac{|2 + 1 - 2 - 10|}{\sqrt{4 + 1 + 4}} = \dfrac{9}{3} = 3\) units.

67.subtopic: Inverse Trigonometric Identities — Sums, Substitution and Telescoping
67.solution:
\(\cot(\cos^{-1}x) = \dfrac{x}{\sqrt{1 - x^2}}\). For \(\theta = \tan^{-1}\dfrac{a}{\sqrt{b^2 - a^2}}\) the hypotenuse is b, so \(\sec\theta = \dfrac{b}{\sqrt{b^2 - a^2}}\).

\(\dfrac{x^2}{1 - x^2} = \dfrac{b^2}{b^2 - a^2}\) gives \(x^2(2b^2 - a^2) = b^2\), so \(x = \dfrac{b}{\sqrt{2b^2 - a^2}}\).

68.subtopic: Composite Functions — f∘g, Iteration and Functional Identities

69.subtopic: Discontinuities of [x], |x| and sgn x — Counting the Points
69.solution:
For \(x > 0\), \(f(x) = 0\); for \(x < 0\), \(f(x) = \dfrac{2x}{x} = 2\). The function is constant on each side, so it is continuous for \(x \neq 0\).

At 0 the right-hand limit is 0 and the left-hand limit 2, so f is discontinuous at \(x = 0\).

70.subtopic: Derivative of One Function with Respect to Another
70.solution:
Put \(x = \tan\theta\). Then \(\dfrac{\sec\theta - 1}{\tan\theta} = \dfrac{1 - \cos\theta}{\sin\theta} = \tan\dfrac{\theta}{2}\), so the first function is \(\dfrac{\theta}{2} = \dfrac{1}{2}\tan^{-1}x\).

\(\dfrac{2x}{1 + x^2} = \sin 2\theta\), so (for \(|x| \le 1\)) the second is \(2\theta = 2\tan^{-1}x\).

The derivative of one with respect to the other is \(\dfrac{1/2}{2} = \dfrac{1}{4}\).

72.solution:
\(\dfrac{dy}{dx} = -\dfrac{x^2}{y^2}\). Differentiating again: \(\dfrac{d^2y}{dx^2} = -\dfrac{2xy^2 - 2x^2y\,y'}{y^4} = -\dfrac{2x(y^3 + x^3)}{y^5} = -\dfrac{12x}{y^5}\).

By symmetry \(\dfrac{d^2x}{dy^2} = -\dfrac{12y}{x^5}\). The product is \(\dfrac{144xy}{x^5y^5} = \dfrac{144}{(xy)^4}\).

So \(m = 144\), \(n = 4\) and \(\dfrac{m}{n} = 36\).

73.solution:
\(y = \cos(p\sin^{-1}x)\), so \(y' = -\dfrac{p\sin(p\sin^{-1}x)}{\sqrt{1 - x^2}}\), that is \(\sqrt{1 - x^2}\,y' = -p\sin(pt)\).

Differentiating again: \(\sqrt{1 - x^2}\,y'' - \dfrac{x}{\sqrt{1 - x^2}}y' = -\dfrac{p^2\cos(pt)}{\sqrt{1 - x^2}}\).

Multiplying by \(\sqrt{1 - x^2}\): \((1 - x^2)y'' - xy' = -p^2y\).

74.subtopic: Rolle's Theorem and Mean Value Theorem

75.subtopic: Tangents, Normals, and the Slope of a Curve
75.solution:
\(2yy' - y - xy' = 0\) gives \(y' = \dfrac{y}{2y - x}\). The tangent is vertical where \(2y - x = 0\).

With \(x = 2y\) the curve gives \(y^2 - 2y^2 + 9 = 0\), so \(y = \pm 3\).

76.solution: \(f'(x) = \cos x + \sin x - k\). The largest value of \(\cos x + \sin x\) is \(\sqrt{2}\), so \(f'(x) < 0\) for all x needs \(k > \sqrt{2}\).

77.subtopic: Trigonometric Integrals - Rational and Substitution Forms
77.solution:
\(\sin 4x = 4\sin x\cos x\cos 2x\), so the integrand is \(\dfrac{1}{4\cos x\cos 2x} = \dfrac{\cos x}{4\cos^2 x\,(1 - 2\sin^2 x)}\).

Put \(s = \sin x\): \(\dfrac{1}{4}\displaystyle\int\dfrac{ds}{(1 - s^2)(1 - 2s^2)}\), and \(\dfrac{1}{(1 - s^2)(1 - 2s^2)} = \dfrac{2}{1 - 2s^2} - \dfrac{1}{1 - s^2}\).

\(\displaystyle\int\dfrac{2\,ds}{1 - 2s^2} = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\log\left|\dfrac{1 + \sqrt{2}s}{1 - \sqrt{2}s}\right|\) and \(\displaystyle\int\dfrac{ds}{1 - s^2} = \dfrac{1}{2}\log\left|\dfrac{1 + s}{1 - s}\right| = \log|\sec x + \tan x|\).

So the integral is \(\dfrac{1}{4\sqrt{2}}\log\left|\dfrac{1 + \sqrt{2}\sin x}{1 - \sqrt{2}\sin x}\right| - \dfrac{1}{4}\log|\sec x + \tan x| + c\).

78.solution:
The integrand is \(2^x\sqrt{(2^x)^2 + 4}\). Put \(t = 2^x\), \(dt = 2^x\log 2\,dx\):

\(\dfrac{1}{\log 2}\displaystyle\int\sqrt{t^2 + 4}\,dt = \dfrac{1}{\log 2}\left[\dfrac{t}{2}\sqrt{t^2 + 4} + 2\log|t + \sqrt{t^2 + 4}|\right] + c\), with \(t = 2^x\).

79.solution:
\(x^2 - 5x + 8 = \left(x - \dfrac{5}{2}\right)^2 + \dfrac{7}{4}\). Using \(\displaystyle\int\dfrac{dx}{u^2 + a^2} = \dfrac{1}{a}\tan^{-1}\dfrac{u}{a}\) with \(a = \dfrac{\sqrt{7}}{2}\):

the integral is \(\dfrac{2}{\sqrt{7}}\tan^{-1}\left(\dfrac{2x - 5}{\sqrt{7}}\right) + c\).

80.solution:
\(4 - 3x - x^2 = (4 + x)(1 - x)\), and \(\dfrac{2x}{(4 + x)(1 - x)} = \dfrac{-8/5}{4 + x} + \dfrac{2/5}{1 - x}\).

Integrating: \(-\dfrac{8}{5}\log|4 + x| - \dfrac{2}{5}\log|1 - x| + c\) (since \(\displaystyle\int\dfrac{dx}{1 - x} = -\log|1 - x|\)).

81.subtopic: Evaluating Definite Integrals — Standard Forms, Algebraic Substitution and By Parts
81.solution:
\(\dfrac{d}{dx}\left(\dfrac{x}{\log x}\right) = \dfrac{1}{\log x} - \dfrac{1}{(\log x)^2}\), so the integral is \(\left[\dfrac{x}{\log x}\right]_2^e = e - \dfrac{2}{\log 2}\).

So \(a = e\) and \(b = -2\).

82.subtopic: Evaluating Definite Integrals — Standard Forms, Algebraic Substitution and By Parts
82.solution:
\(\dfrac{1}{1 + 4^x} = \dfrac{4^{-x}}{1 + 4^{-x}}\), whose integral is \(-\dfrac{1}{\log 4}\log(1 + 4^{-x})\).

So \(\displaystyle\int_0^k = \dfrac{1}{\log 4}\log\dfrac{2}{1 + 4^{-k}} = \log_2\sqrt{\dfrac{2}{1 + 4^{-k}}}\).

Setting this to \(\log_2\dfrac{4}{3}\): \(\dfrac{2}{1 + 4^{-k}} = \dfrac{16}{9}\), so \(4^{-k} = \dfrac{1}{8}\), \(2^{-2k} = 2^{-3}\) and \(k = \dfrac{3}{2}\).

83.subtopic: Area Under a Curve — Between a Curve and an Axis
83.solution:
\(\displaystyle\int x\sin\dfrac{x}{2}\,dx = -2x\cos\dfrac{x}{2} + 4\sin\dfrac{x}{2}\). On \([0, 2\pi]\) the sine is positive, and on \([2\pi, 4\pi]\) negative.

\(\displaystyle\int_0^{2\pi}x\sin\dfrac{x}{2}\,dx = -4\pi\cos\pi = 4\pi\).

\(\displaystyle\int_{2\pi}^{4\pi}x\sin\dfrac{x}{2}\,dx = (-8\pi\cos 2\pi) - (-4\pi\cos\pi) = -8\pi - 4\pi = -12\pi\), contributing \(12\pi\) to the area.

Area \(= 4\pi + 12\pi = 16\pi\).

84.subtopic: Area Between Two Curves — Intersections First
84.solution:
They meet where \(k^2x^2 = 4kx\), at \(x = 0\) and \(x = \dfrac{4}{k}\).

Area \(= \displaystyle\int_0^{4/k}\left(2\sqrt{kx} - kx\right)dx = \dfrac{4\sqrt{k}}{3}\left(\dfrac{4}{k}\right)^{3/2} - \dfrac{k}{2}\cdot\dfrac{16}{k^2} = \dfrac{32}{3k} - \dfrac{8}{k} = \dfrac{8}{3k}\).

\(\dfrac{8}{3k} = \dfrac{2k}{3}\) gives \(k^2 = 4\), so \(k = 2\).

85.solution: \(\dfrac{dy}{y + 3} = \dfrac{dx}{2x}\) gives \(\log(y + 3) = \dfrac{1}{2}\log x + \log c\), that is \((y + 3)^2 = c^2x\): a family of parabolas.

86.solution:
Divide by \(xy^6\): \(y^{-6}\dfrac{dy}{dx} + \dfrac{y^{-5}}{x} = x^2\). With \(v = y^{-5}\), \(\dfrac{dv}{dx} = -5y^{-6}\dfrac{dy}{dx}\), so \(\dfrac{dv}{dx} - \dfrac{5v}{x} = -5x^2\).

The integrating factor is \(x^{-5}\): \(\dfrac{d}{dx}(vx^{-5}) = -5x^{-3}\), so \(vx^{-5} = \dfrac{5}{2}x^{-2} + c\).

\(\dfrac{1}{y^5} = \dfrac{5}{2}x^3 + cx^5\).

87.subtopic: Scalar Triple Product, Coplanarity, and Volume
87.solution:
Coplanar vectors have \([\bar{a}\ \bar{b}\ \bar{c}] = 0\):

\(\begin{vmatrix} 1 & 1 & 1 \\ 1 & -1 & 2 \\ x & x - 2 & -1 \end{vmatrix} = (1 - 2x + 4) - (-1 - 2x) + (x - 2 + x) = 4 + 2x = 0\), so \(x = -2\).

88.subtopic: Scalar Triple Product, Coplanarity, and Volume
88.solution:
A triple product with a repeated vector vanishes, so \([\bar{a}\ \ \bar{a} + \bar{b}\ \ \bar{a} \times \bar{b}] = [\bar{a}\ \ \bar{b}\ \ \bar{a} \times \bar{b}] = (\bar{a} \times \bar{b})\cdot(\bar{a} \times \bar{b}) = |\bar{a} \times \bar{b}|^2\).

\(|\bar{a} \times \bar{b}|^2 = |\bar{a}|^2|\bar{b}|^2 - (\bar{a}\cdot\bar{b})^2 = 144 - 64 = 80\).

89.solution:
\(\bar{a}\cdot\bar{b} = 0\) and \(\bar{b}\cdot\bar{c} = -\dfrac{1}{2}\). From \((\bar{a} + \bar{c})\cdot(\bar{b} + \bar{c}) = 0\): \(0 + \bar{a}\cdot\bar{c} - \dfrac{1}{2} + 1 = 0\), so \(\bar{a}\cdot\bar{c} = -\dfrac{1}{2}\).

\((\bar{a} - \bar{c})\cdot(\bar{b} - \bar{c}) = \bar{a}\cdot\bar{b} - \bar{a}\cdot\bar{c} - \bar{c}\cdot\bar{b} + 1 = 0 + \dfrac{1}{2} + \dfrac{1}{2} + 1 = 2\). (A) gives \(-1\) and (C) gives \(-1\).

90.subtopic: Scalar Triple Product, Coplanarity, and Volume

91.subtopic: Scalar Triple Product, Coplanarity, and Volume
91.solution:
\(\bar{b} \times \bar{c} = (3 \cdot 4 - (-2)(1),\ (-2)(-3) - 1 \cdot 4,\ 1 \cdot 1 - 3(-3)) = (14, 2, 10)\), with magnitude \(\sqrt{300} = 10\sqrt{3}\) (the base area).

Volume \(= |\bar{a}\cdot(\bar{b} \times \bar{c})| = |-28 + 10 + 30| = 12\).

Altitude \(= \dfrac{12}{10\sqrt{3}} = \dfrac{2\sqrt{3}}{5}\).

93.solution:
On the first line \(z = 1\); on the second \(y = 2\). So the point has \(y = 2\), \(z = 1\).

Second line with \(z = 1\): \(\dfrac{x - 6}{2} = 0\), \(x = 6\). Check on the first: \(\dfrac{6 - 3}{3} = 1 = \dfrac{2 - 3}{-1}\). The point is \((6, 2, 1)\).

94.subtopic: Tetrahedron Geometry — Centroid, Volume, and Vertices
94.solution:
The centroid is the average of the four vertices: \(\dfrac{a + 3}{4} = 1\), \(\dfrac{b + 3}{4} = 2\), \(\dfrac{c + 5}{4} = -1\). So \(a = 1\), \(b = 5\), \(c = -9\).

Distance \(= \sqrt{1 + 25 + 81} = \sqrt{107}\) units.

96.subtopic: Formulation and Special Cases — Word Problems and Infinitely Many Optima
96.solution: z must be equal at the two corners: \(3p = p + q\), so \(q = 2p\), that is \(p = \dfrac{q}{2}\). (Then z at \((0, 3)\) is \(3q = 6p\), larger than \(3p\), so these are minima.)

97.subtopic: Parameter Estimation and the Probability Ratio

99.subtopic: The Binomial Setting and Probability Mass Function
99.solution: \(P(X \le 2) = \dfrac{1 + 5 + 10}{32} = \dfrac{1}{2}\) and \(P(X \ge 3) = \dfrac{10 + 5 + 1}{32} = \dfrac{1}{2}\). They are equal (the distribution is symmetric).

100.subtopic: Conditional Probability, Independence and Bayes' Theorem

103.solution: The minute hand turns \(360^\circ\) in \(3600\) s: \(\dfrac{360}{3600} = 0.1^\circ\) per second.

104.subtopic: Uniform Circular Motion — Centripetal Acceleration, Banking
104.solution: Radial acceleration \(= \dfrac{V^2}{r}\) and tangential acceleration \(= r\alpha\). Their ratio is \(\dfrac{V^2}{r^2\alpha}\).

105.solution:
Momentum before: \(MV\hat{i} + 2M(3V)\hat{j} = MV\hat{i} + 6MV\hat{j}\). After, the mass is \(3M\):

\(\vec{v} = \dfrac{MV\hat{i} + 6MV\hat{j}}{3M} = \dfrac{V}{3}\hat{i} + 2V\hat{j}\).

106.solution:
Angular momentum is conserved: \(I\omega = 2I\omega'\), so \(\omega' = \dfrac{\omega}{2}\).

Initial KE \(= \dfrac{1}{2}I\omega^2\); final KE \(= \dfrac{1}{2}(2I)\dfrac{\omega^2}{4} = \dfrac{I\omega^2}{4}\). The loss is \(\dfrac{I\omega^2}{4}\).

107.subtopic: Moment of Inertia and Radius of Gyration

108.subtopic: Variation of g with Depth, Altitude, Density, and Latitude

109.solution:
Volume is conserved: \(512r^3 = R^3\), so \(r = \dfrac{R}{8}\).

Total surface area \(= 512 \times 4\pi\dfrac{R^2}{64} = 8 \times 4\pi R^2\). Surface energy is proportional to area, so it becomes \(8E\).

110.solution:
Water wets both the tube wall and the wire (contact angle about 0), so surface tension pulls upward along both circles, a total length \(2\pi(R + r)\). The raised water fills the ring of area \(\pi(R^2 - r^2)\).

\(T \cdot 2\pi(R + r) = h\rho g\,\pi(R^2 - r^2)\) gives \(h = \dfrac{2T}{(R - r)\rho g}\).

111.solution: \(27r^3 = R^3\) gives \(R = 3r\). Excess pressure \(\dfrac{2T}{r}\) is inversely proportional to the radius, so it becomes \(\dfrac{9}{3} = 3\) units.

112.subtopic: Radiation — Stefan, Wien, Newton's Law of Cooling, Black Body
112.solution:
By Newton's law of cooling the excess over the surroundings falls by the same factor in equal times.

First stage: from \(50^\circ\) above to \(30^\circ\) above, a factor of \(\dfrac{3}{5}\), in 7 min. Second stage: from \(30^\circ\) above to \(18^\circ\) above, again a factor of \(\dfrac{3}{5}\). So it also takes \(7\) minutes. (The average-rate form gives the same answer.)

113.subtopic: Isothermal, Adiabatic, Isobaric, and Isochoric Processes
113.solution:
For an adiabatic change \(P^{1 - \gamma}T^\gamma\) is constant, so \(P \propto T^{\gamma/(\gamma - 1)}\).

For a rigid diatomic gas \(\gamma = \dfrac{7}{5}\): \(x = \dfrac{7/5}{2/5} = 3.5\).

114.subtopic: Average KE, Equipartition, and Specific Heats
114.solution:
At constant pressure: \(\Delta Q = nC_p\Delta T = \dfrac{7}{2}nR\Delta T\), \(\Delta U = nC_v\Delta T = \dfrac{5}{2}nR\Delta T\) and \(\Delta W = nR\Delta T\).

\(\Delta W : \Delta U : \Delta Q = 1 : \dfrac{5}{2} : \dfrac{7}{2} = 2 : 5 : 7\).

115.subtopic: Average KE, Equipartition, and Specific Heats
115.solution:
Per mole, the kinetic energy of bulk motion, \(\dfrac{1}{2}mv^2\), becomes internal energy \(\dfrac{3}{2}R\Delta T\) (monoatomic gas).

\(\Delta T = \dfrac{mv^2}{3R}\).

117.subtopic: Average KE, Equipartition, and Specific Heats
117.solution: \(C_v = \dfrac{R}{0.4} = \dfrac{5}{2}R\), which is the molar specific heat of a rigid diatomic gas (5 degrees of freedom).

118.solution:
\(T = 2\pi\sqrt{\dfrac{l}{g_{eff}}}\), so \(\dfrac{1}{T^2} \propto g_{eff}\): \(g\) at rest, \(g + a\) going up, \(g - a\) going down.

\(\dfrac{1}{T_2^2} + \dfrac{1}{T_3^2} = \dfrac{2}{T_1^2}\), so \(T_1^2 = \dfrac{2T_2^2T_3^2}{T_2^2 + T_3^2}\) and \(T_1 = \dfrac{\sqrt{2}T_2T_3}{\sqrt{T_2^2 + T_3^2}}\).

119.subtopic: SHM Energy — Kinetic, Potential, and Total
119.solution:
Total energy \(= 2 + 1.2 = 3.2\) J \(= \dfrac{1}{2}m\omega^2A^2\), with \(\omega = 2\pi \times \dfrac{16}{\pi} = 32\) rad/s.

\(\dfrac{1}{2} \times 0.4 \times 1024 \times A^2 = 3.2\) gives \(A^2 = \dfrac{1}{64}\), so \(A = 0.125\) m.

120.subtopic: SHM Kinematics — Displacement, Velocity, Phase, and Damping
120.solution: The period is \(1\) s and the motion starts at an extreme (\(x = A\) at \(t = 0\)). The speed is greatest first at the mean position, a quarter period later: \(\dfrac{1}{4}\) s.

121.solution:
First overtones at length L: open pipe \(\dfrac{v}{L}\), closed pipe \(\dfrac{3v}{4L}\). Their difference \(\dfrac{v}{4L} = 3\), so \(\dfrac{v}{L} = 12\) Hz. (The fundamentals, \(\dfrac{v}{2L}\) and \(\dfrac{v}{4L}\), also differ by \(\dfrac{v}{4L}\).)

After the change, comparing fundamentals: open pipe of length \(\dfrac{L}{3}\) gives \(\dfrac{3v}{2L} = 18\) Hz and closed pipe of length \(3L\) gives \(\dfrac{v}{12L} = 1\) Hz, so \(17\) beats, option (C).

If both pipes are still sounding their first overtone, the frequencies are \(\dfrac{3v}{L} = 36\) Hz and \(\dfrac{v}{4L} = 3\) Hz, giving 33 beats, which is not an option.
121.note: read literally (both pipes still in their first overtone) the answer is 33 beats, which is not an option; 17 (C) comes from comparing FUNDAMENTALS after the change. Kept PRIVATE.

122.solution:
\(f_p = \dfrac{p}{2L}\sqrt{\dfrac{T}{\mu}}\), with \(\mu \propto r^2\), so \(\sqrt{\mu_1} = 2\sqrt{\mu_2}\).

First overtone of wire 1 (\(p = 2\)) equals second overtone of wire 2 (\(p = 3\)): \(\dfrac{2}{2L_1}\cdot\dfrac{1}{2\sqrt{\mu_2}} = \dfrac{3}{2L_2}\cdot\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{\mu_2}}\), so \(\dfrac{1}{2L_1} = \dfrac{3}{2L_2}\) and \(\dfrac{L_1}{L_2} = \dfrac{1}{3}\).

123.subtopic: Progressive Wave, Wave Equation, and Velocity
123.solution:
Compare with \(A\sin(\omega t - kx + \phi)\): amplitude \(3\) m, \(\omega = \dfrac{\pi}{3}\) and \(k = \dfrac{\pi}{5}\).

\(\lambda = \dfrac{2\pi}{k} = 10\) m, \(f = \dfrac{\omega}{2\pi} = \dfrac{1}{6}\) Hz and \(v = \dfrac{\omega}{k} = \dfrac{5}{3}\) m/s. Only (C) is correct.

124.subtopic: Doppler Effect — Moving Source and Observer
124.solution:
Approaching: \(n_1 = \dfrac{nV}{V - V_s}\); receding: \(n_2 = \dfrac{nV}{V + V_s}\).

\(n_1 - n_2 = nV\left(\dfrac{1}{V - V_s} - \dfrac{1}{V + V_s}\right) = \dfrac{2nVV_s}{V^2 - V_s^2}\).

125.solution: By Gauss's law the flux through a closed surface is \(\dfrac{q}{\epsilon_0}\), set only by the enclosed charge. Enlarging the sphere does not change it.

126.solution:
For a sphere \(\dfrac{V}{A} = \dfrac{\frac{4}{3}\pi R^3}{4\pi R^2} = \dfrac{R}{3}\), so \(R = \dfrac{3V}{A}\).

\(C = 4\pi\epsilon_0R = 12\pi\epsilon_0\dfrac{V}{A}\).

127.solution: Each capacitor keeps its charge \(CV\) and its potential V. In series the potentials add, giving \(nV\). The energy is \(n \times \dfrac{1}{2}CV^2\) in both arrangements, since no charge has moved, so it is unchanged.

129.solution: With the same driving cell across a longer wire, the potential drop per unit length (potential gradient) falls. Balancing the same emf then needs a longer length, so the balancing length increases.

130.solution:
The bridge is balanced, since \(\dfrac{15}{3} = \dfrac{20}{4}\), so no current flows in the branch BD (the \(6\,\Omega\) resistor and G).

The current divides between path ABC (\(15 + 3 = 18\,\Omega\)) and path ADC (\(20 + 4 = 24\,\Omega\)). Through the \(15\,\Omega\) resistor: \(2.1 \times \dfrac{24}{18 + 24} = 1.2\) A.

131.chapter: Magnetic Fields Due to Electric Current
131.subtopic: Magnetic Moment of Current Loop and Galvanometer Instruments
131.solution:
The wire length is unchanged: \(N\pi D = N'\pi(2D)\), so \(N' = \dfrac{N}{2}\).

\(m = NIA \propto ND^2\): original \(ND^2\), new \(\dfrac{N}{2}(4D^2) = 2ND^2\). The ratio original : new is \(1 : 2\).

132.chapter: Magnetic Fields Due to Electric Current
132.subtopic: Force on Current-Carrying Conductor and Parallel Wires
132.solution:
The currents are opposite, so the wires repel and CD is pushed upward. The force per unit length is \(\dfrac{\mu_0I_1I_2}{2\pi r}\).

CD stays suspended when this balances its weight per unit length \(\lambda g\): \(\lambda = \dfrac{\mu_0I_1I_2}{2\pi rg}\).

133.chapter: Magnetic Fields Due to Electric Current
133.solution:
For opposite currents the two fields point the same way at the midpoint and add. Each wire is \(1.5\) m away:

\(B = \dfrac{\mu_0}{2\pi(1.5)}(3 + 4.5) = \dfrac{\mu_0 \times 7.5}{3\pi} = \dfrac{5\mu_0}{2\pi}\).

134.subtopic: Faraday's and Lenz's Laws — Induced EMF, Current, and Charge
134.solution: The magnitude of the induced emf is \(\dfrac{n(\phi_2 - \phi_1)}{t}\) and the total resistance is \(R + 2R = 3R\). The current is \(\dfrac{n(\phi_2 - \phi_1)}{3Rt}\).

135.subtopic: Reactance — Inductive, Capacitive, and Single-Element Circuits
135.solution: \(X_C = \dfrac{1}{2\pi fC}\). Lowering C raises \(X_C\), so the current falls and the bulb dims. Lowering f also raises \(X_C\), so again the bulb dims.

136.subtopic: Power in AC Circuit — Average, Factor, Wattless
136.solution: Apparent power \(= V_{rms}I_{rms}\) and true power \(= V_{rms}I_{rms}\cos\phi\). Their ratio is \(\dfrac{1}{\cos\phi} = \dfrac{Z}{R}\).

137.subtopic: Power in AC Circuit — Average, Factor, Wattless
137.solution: \(I_{rms} = \dfrac{220}{33} = \dfrac{20}{3}\) A, and true power \(= I_{rms}^2R = \dfrac{400}{9} \times 18 = 800\) W.

138.solution: An ideal transformer passes all the power on: \(I_s = \dfrac{P}{V_s} = \dfrac{4400}{3300} = \dfrac{4}{3}\) A. (The number of turns is not needed.)

139.solution: With \(I = I_0\sin\omega t\), the secondary emf is \(M\dfrac{dI}{dt}\), whose peak is \(M\omega I_0 = 1 \times 2\pi \times 50 \times \dfrac{2}{\pi} = 200\) V.

140.subtopic: Prism — Deviation, Dispersion, and Refractive Index
140.solution:
For a thin prism \(\delta = (\mu - 1)A\). In air \(\mu = \dfrac{3}{2}\), so \(\delta = \dfrac{A}{2}\).

In water the relative index is \(\dfrac{3/2}{4/3} = \dfrac{9}{8}\), so \(\delta' = \dfrac{A}{8} = \dfrac{\delta}{4}\).

141.subtopic: Young's Double Slit — Fringe Width, Positions and Shifts
141.solution: The nth dark band is at \(y = \dfrac{(2n - 1)\lambda D}{2d}\). Opposite a slit, \(y = \dfrac{d}{2}\). With \(n = 4\): \(\dfrac{7\lambda D}{2d} = \dfrac{d}{2}\), so \(\lambda = \dfrac{d^2}{7D}\).

142.subtopic: Young's Double Slit — Fringe Width, Positions and Shifts
142.solution: A minimum opposite a slit means \(\dfrac{(2n - 1)\lambda D}{2d} = \dfrac{d}{2}\), so \(\lambda = \dfrac{d^2}{(2n - 1)D}\): inversely proportional to \(D, 3D, 5D, \ldots\)

143.subtopic: Single Slit Diffraction and Resolving Power
143.solution:
At the Rayleigh limit the angular separation is \(\theta = \dfrac{1.22\lambda}{a}\), and in the focal plane the separation is \(f\theta\):

\(\dfrac{1.22 \times 5000\ \mathrm{\mathring{A}} \times 25}{5} = 30500\) \(\mathrm{\mathring{A}}\).

144.chapter: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter
144.subtopic: Photoelectric Effect — Stopping Potential, Threshold, and Work Function
144.solution:
Photon energies: \(\dfrac{hc}{\lambda_1} = \dfrac{2}{3}\cdot\dfrac{hc}{\lambda_2}\). With work function \(\phi\): \(E_2 = \dfrac{hc}{\lambda_2} - \phi\) and \(E_1 = \dfrac{2}{3}\cdot\dfrac{hc}{\lambda_2} - \phi\).

\(E_1 = \dfrac{2}{3}(E_2 + \phi) - \phi = \dfrac{2}{3}E_2 - \dfrac{\phi}{3} < \dfrac{2E_2}{3}\).

145.chapter: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter
145.subtopic: de Broglie Wavelength and Matter Waves

146.solution:
The magnetic force provides the centripetal force: \(qvB = \dfrac{mv^2}{r}\), so \(r = \dfrac{mv}{qB}\). Bohr's condition: \(mvr = \dfrac{nh}{2\pi}\).

Then \(\dfrac{(mv)^2}{qB} = \dfrac{nh}{2\pi}\), so \((mv)^2 = \dfrac{nhqB}{2\pi}\). The magnetic force does no work, so the energy is kinetic: \(E = \dfrac{(mv)^2}{2m} = \dfrac{nhqB}{4\pi m}\).

147.solution: \(r \propto n^2\) and \(V \propto \dfrac{1}{n}\). So \(Vr \propto n\), and \(\dfrac{1}{Vr} \propto \dfrac{1}{n}\). (\(V^2r\) does not depend on n and \(Vr^2 \propto n^3\).)

148.subtopic: Transistors — BJT, CE Amplifier, and Gain

149.solution: A NAND gate is an AND gate followed by NOT: \(Y = \overline{A \cdot B}\).

150.subtopic: Band Theory, Doping, and Semiconductor Types
150.solution: In an insulator the forbidden gap is very large (more than about 3 eV), so electrons cannot reach the conduction band, which remains empty.
